persons.name: Kaelyn
persons.harm: From about age 19 she was catfished for years by a friend who invented personas (a harasser, a love interest 'Tyler' who faked his suicide, and his sister), leaving her with years of guilt and grief; the friend also pressed her to send money for a vehicle.

quotes.quote: And I really don't remember what excuse she gave me, but it was something that I had believed because I don't even know. I was very impressionable.

I wasn't trying to ruin her reputation or her friendship that she may have developed, and I was trying to just let things go, because I thought, you know, in my head that this was just like a one-time thing that she had done and we all make mistakes, so I didn't want to. I just, I wasn't trying to ruin her life. So I didn't really say anything.
So anytime I would talk about Tyler or like cry about him, he would just be like, I don't know why you care, you never met met him or you know he was just very like emotionally abusive

persons.outcome_quote: No, I don't know if she just deleted her whole account or if she just deleted me, but I saw that we're not friends on Facebook anymore
persons.notes: Reason 'other' = did not want to ruin the perpetrator's life/reputation. Discovery came through her own checking (Facebook profile, asking the perpetrator's ex-husband); the perpetrator later admitted it privately. She went public on TikTok (6.5M views); no institution involved. She says she will 'probably' go back to counseling, but nothing shows the harm was raised with a counselor. A later boyfriend is described as 'very like emotionally abusive' (dismissing her grief) - a separate harm with no further story; noted here, not a separate record. Ex-husband's and Tiffany's statements are relayed by Kaelyn, not heard on air, so evidence coded person_account_alone.

persons.name: Tiffany (catfished by the same perpetrator)
persons.harm: Catfished by the same woman, who (per Kaelyn) made her believe a little girl had died and led to money being sent to a nonexistent family; she then catfished the perpetrator back on an MTV Catfish episode.

quotes.quote: I come to find out that she, [perpetrator] had catfished multiple people, and one of them who her name is Tiffany, ended up catfishing her back in order to get revenge, and that was what the whole catfish episode was about.

persons.outcome_quote: So because it was like kids were involved in like pictures of those kids, they took the episode down because they MTV didn't want like any legal action with that.
persons.notes: Told only second-hand through Kaelyn, who hedges ('I might be saying this wrong'). The MTV TV show is media, not an institution with a duty to respond, so not coded as a contact. Not the podcast host (also named Tiffany).

persons.name: Jez
persons.harm: Lured to a Denver restaurant through a fake online-dating profile by a man who then sat beside her pretending to be a stranger, pushed drinks and repeatedly tried to get her to leave with him; staff said he did this to many women, who appeared more intoxicated than expected and usually left with him.
persons.perpetrator_role: an unknown man using a fake dating profile

contacts.institution: Old Chicago restaurant (downtown Denver) server and bartender
contacts.when: during the evening, about 30 minutes after she arrived
contacts.what_was_asked: Nothing; the staff approached her themselves.
contacts.what_institution_did: A server warned her in the restroom that the man next to her had set up the meeting and described his pattern; the staff had chilled her shots, watched over her, bought her dinner, let her stay for hours and the bartender walked her to her car.
contacts.quote: And I just like kind of got like this sinking feeling of like, she goes, okay, this is gonna sound crazy. But whatever reason you're here, it's because of him. He got you here.
contacts.what_happened_next: She refused to leave with him and he left angry; she stayed about four hours and was walked to her car.
contacts.notes: Coded as an institution (type other) because a restaurant has some power over its premises; staff said they had no proof and did not know who he was ('He always pays with cash'). If a restaurant is not counted as an institution, the outcome would be not_protected.

contacts.institution: Denver-area police (non-emergency call)
contacts.when: the same night or soon after
contacts.what_was_asked: To let police know about the man's behavior.
contacts.what_institution_did: Told her there was nothing they could do because nothing illegal had happened, unless he followed or stalked her.
contacts.quote: And I remember they were like, well, I remember they were nice. They were just, they were like, well, there's nothing we can really do about that. They're not technically doing anything illegal.
contacts.what_happened_next: Nothing further; the man was never identified.

persons.outcome_quote: And even though you got lucky and the staff there were caring enough to insert themselves and make sure that you were okay, that's still a really scary thing when you're by yourself.
persons.decisive_work_quote: And because we don't really have any proof of like what he's doing, it's not like there's something, you know, like they were doing the most that they could to try and like protect women they felt were at risk, essentially. Like when he chilled the shots.
persons.time_to_first_effective_action: the same evening (staff intervened during the encounter)
persons.notes: Partly protected: staff intervention kept her safe that night, but the man was unaffected and police took no step. Outcome quote is the host's summary. Jez mentions an earlier harm by 'a person who was a sociopath' and 'traumatic experiences earlier in my life' with no story; not a separate record. Story later featured on Crime Junkie (s6-e5 intro).

persons.name: Ilyse (harassing caller)
persons.harm: As a newer therapist she answered her work phone to a man posing as a prospective client who asked sexual questions and sought a relationship with her; when she posted about it another therapist blamed her.

quotes.quote: And I politely, you know, I had my people pleasing response come up and I was just like, you know, that's not ethical. I'm happy to refer you to another therapist if this is feeling like you would not be able to work with me.

persons.outcome_quote: And so I said, as a young female therapist, I don't answer my work phone when it rings because I've received harassing phone calls.
persons.notes: Expert guest in an expert episode. The therapist who blamed her commented in an online post; no professional body involved. She mentions a 'sexual trauma history' with no story.

persons.name: Ilyse (COVID-denier troll)
persons.harm: A troll reposted the same comment on her Instagram under several profiles after she deleted it, then called her work line and left a harassing message.

quotes.quote: And literally the only response that I got was really pretty victim blamey, shamey, and just said, I keep my Instagram account private and wouldn't write anything that I wouldn't want clients to see.

persons.outcome_quote: And so I am still working on those safety measures.
persons.notes: She deleted the comments herself; no report to Instagram or police is mentioned. The 'victim blamey' response came from a therapist marketing group (peers, not an institution). She took her phone number off Instagram.

persons.name: Jill (harassment after viral post)
persons.harm: After her 'Fuck COVID School' blog post went viral she got 'you should kill yourself' comments and abusive private messages.

quotes.quote: And here's the thing, I was mentally healthy enough to like disregard that.

persons.outcome_quote: And so that was, I think, more upsetting for me, not in like how it made me feel personally, but how it made me feel thinking about that person going on and saying that to somebody else who may not be in as good of a place.
persons.notes: Reason 'other' = chose to disregard the messages. Earlier criticism of her apartment post (some commenters later apologized; she discussed it with her therapist) is not coded as a harm: she says the pushback did not hurt her much. Her January suicidality was not caused by anyone.

persons.name: Charlie (harassment after miscarriage post)
persons.harm: After a viral post about his and his wife's miscarriage he received 'you should go kill yourself' messages and comments that God was punishing him.

quotes.quote: But to see commenters like that faceless nameless commenters come in and say that God wanted it this way and I deserved it Was something that I it was hard for me not to internalize at some point

persons.outcome_quote: But to see commenters like that faceless nameless commenters come in and say that God wanted it this way and I deserved it Was something that I it was hard for me not to internalize at some point
persons.notes: His wife's poor medical care during the miscarriage (lack of instruments in that state) is not abuse and is not coded.

persons.name: Charlie (trolling over Harry Styles post)

quotes.quote: And I'm okay with it. I absolve you. I release you from having to follow me and go ahead and leave.

persons.name: J.E. (Tree of Life shooting)
persons.harm: A member of the Tree of Life congregation whose community was attacked by a gunman on 27 October 2018; 11 people they knew were murdered (their stepfather was the synagogue's former executive director), leaving them with grief and PTSD.

contacts.institution: J.E.'s psychiatrist
contacts.when: a few days after the shooting
contacts.what_institution_did: Saw J.E. for a session a few days after the shooting.
contacts.quote: I was seeing a psychiatrist, but I was able to luckily have a session with them a few, like a few days after the shooting to be able to start processing it.
contacts.what_happened_next: Writing became J.E.'s main way to cope; months later the harassing calls began.

persons.outcome_quote: I couldn't step foot into any synagogue for a really long time. It's still really hard for me to do it.
persons.notes: The only institutional contact for this harm is therapeutic, and a therapy session is not protective action, so outcome is not_protected. The season never says whether the shooter was arrested or tried. The Vanity Fair essay J.E. read on air counts as document_read_on_air. Also mentions being called a slur by Catholic-school boys at age five (no further story; not a separate record).

persons.name: J.E. (the Caller)
persons.harm: From February 2019, months after the shooting, an anonymous caller left hundreds of antisemitic, homophobic and transphobic voicemails on their stepfather's phones aimed at J.E. by their first name, with threats to shoot, behead and sexually assault them. The calls ran in two waves until her arrest in March 2023; a forum thread also said J.E. should be raped.

contacts.institution: Pittsburgh police (J.E.'s precinct)
contacts.when: February 2019, the day the threats came to light
contacts.what_was_asked: Protection and investigation of the death threats.
contacts.what_institution_did: Took the report seriously, kept a police car outside 24 hours a day for about a week, then increased patrols for about two weeks.
contacts.quote: For the first, at least the first couple of days, maybe slightly under a week there, was actually a police car parked outside for 24 hours.
contacts.what_happened_next: The calls did not stop; the case was referred up.
contacts.notes: Temporary protection only. The victim impact statement read on air (23-wcn @ 15:07) says the same. J.E. praised the first officer.

contacts.institution: Allegheny County police and the FBI (Pittsburgh), with an FBI liaison
contacts.what_institution_did: Took over the case and set up an FBI liaison to contact with each new call, but could not trace the rerouted number. By late 2020 the investigation was open but 'pretty much dormant'.
contacts.quote: The calls didn't stop. They, I mean, the case was immediately sort of like sent up to Allegheny PD, which is like the county PD as well as the FBI.
contacts.what_happened_next: Calls went on for six to eight months, then paused; they resumed in 2022.
contacts.notes: Dormancy: 'technically it was an open FBI investigation, but it was pretty much dormant' (13-wcn @ 10:48-11:53).

contacts.institution: local detectives assigned to the case
contacts.what_was_asked: Updates on the case; J.E. also sent screenshots of a forum thread threatening them.
contacts.what_institution_did: Rarely returned J.E.'s calls. J.E. had to read the forum threats aloud to an older detective who did not understand the internet, and later said local police did not take the case seriously.
contacts.quote: I called the detectives assigned to the case with persistence, begging for updates. My calls were rarely returned.
contacts.what_happened_next: No progress locally.
contacts.notes: Also: 'it was clear to me that local law enforcement didn't take it seriously ... to try to have to make my case over and over again to have to explain why something like this was anti-Semitic' (33-wcn @ 15:07). Could also be coded disbelieved. This later account differs from the early-2020 one ('they did take it really seriously', s6-e6 @ 18:49-19:51), which was about the first officer.

contacts.institution: J.E.'s editor/boss at a remote contract reporting job
contacts.what_was_asked: Time off shifts to speak with police and investigators.
contacts.what_institution_did: J.E. lost the job shortly after telling the editor, and believes this was the likely reason.
contacts.quote: I lost my job shortly after I told my then editor I'd have to step away to speak to investigators about what was happening.
contacts.what_happened_next: J.E.'s world 'became smaller'; they later found another job in their field.
contacts.notes: J.E. hedges: 'I can't say for certain, but I likely lost a contract job ... because I had to say to my boss' (13-wcn @ 17:06). In s6-e6 @ 24:01 J.E. said the contract 'was already going to be like a temporary gig'. Coded on J.E.'s own attribution; unclear would also be defensible.

contacts.institution: Anti-Defamation League (ADL)
contacts.what_was_asked: To get the case to the FBI's attention.
contacts.what_institution_did: Took the case up and pushed it to the FBI's attention after J.E.'s and their mother's own work.
contacts.quote: At least a couple were from the ADL who were instrumental in elevating this case to the FBI's attention. After all the legwork that I did and my mom did, they really brought it to their attention.
contacts.what_happened_next: The Miami FBI field office investigated.
contacts.notes: Advocacy organization, coded as type other.

contacts.institution: FBI Miami field office
contacts.what_institution_did: Investigated the second wave, identified the caller as a woman living in California and arrested her in March 2023.
contacts.quote: And then I just remember in March of 2023 receiving a call, I think it was first from my mom and then from the FBI liaison, who was one of the agents saying that she had been arrested.
contacts.what_happened_next: She was released on bond, then rearrested on a domestic violence charge and extradited to Florida.
contacts.notes: Recorded under police because the codes have no federal-law-enforcement type. The mother's call-recording app helped build the evidence.

contacts.institution: federal court (bond)
contacts.what_institution_did: Released her on bond.
contacts.quote: I do know that she was let out on bond. So even though she had been arrested, she was still allowed to live free in the public.
contacts.what_happened_next: She was later rearrested for throwing a heavy object at her partner and extradited to Florida.
contacts.notes: Charges stayed in place but she was not detained; unclear would also be defensible.

contacts.institution: US Attorney's office, Southern District of Florida
contacts.what_institution_did: Prosecuted with forensic evidence and hundreds of recordings; she pleaded guilty, and the prosecution played a montage of her threats at sentencing.
contacts.quote: She did plead guilty. The majority of cases that are brought to court, the defendant does plead guilty.
contacts.what_happened_next: Sentencing hearing in Miami with victim impact statements.

contacts.institution: federal court in Miami (sentencing judge)
contacts.what_institution_did: Rejected the defense's 12-month proposal and sentenced her to 32 months plus three years of supervised release, crediting J.E.'s statement about the premeditation.
contacts.quote: The judge delivered his sentence. In the end, she was given 32 months with time served. So that's a few years with three years of supervised release.
contacts.what_happened_next: A restitution hearing was offered and J.E. declined; the defense appeal was reportedly not pursued.

persons.outcome_quote: Meaning that after she's released, if she tries to contact us, she'll be arrested and imprisoned.
persons.decisive_work_quote: The agents who essentially investigated the case and were able to identify who this caller was were really, really wonderful.
persons.time_to_first_effective_action: about four years after the first police report (report February 2019; arrest March 2023)
persons.notes: The arrest ended the calls, so the outcome is protected (J.E. calls the sense of security temporary). harmed_by_institution_ever is true only because of the employer contact, which rests on J.E.'s hedged attribution. Decisive work could arguably be family_or_friends: the mother recorded the calls to build 'forensically irrefutable' evidence and J.E. pressed persistently, and the ADL elevated the case. I chose institution because the story credits the FBI with identifying the caller. J.E. was on long therapy waitlists and uninsured during the first wave; this is not coded as a contact. Months: February 2019 to March 2023 = 49. The court documentation cited on air counts 238 recorded calls.

persons.perpetrator_role: the elderly homeowner advertising the room

quotes.quote: I think we lied to just said we found another place. I felt like if we made him mad, that would have been bad news.

coder_notes: Season 6 holds seven numbered episodes plus three 'WCN Presents: J.E. S6 Updates' parts (in s06_03 and s06_04). Episodes 3 and 4 are expert and guest-panel episodes, and their guests' own harassment experiences are coded as update_or_listener_story. Episode 7 is the host's own story. Only J.E.'s stalking case shows substantial institutional involvement. Judgment calls: (1) Jez - Old Chicago restaurant staff coded as an institution (type other); otherwise not_protected. (2) J.E. - the employer contact is coded blamed_punished on J.E.'s hedged attribution. (3) Tree of Life victims - separate records only for the seven victims described individually; police response coded unclear because the season does not describe the shooter's arrest or prosecution. (4) Jill's apartment-post criticism is not coded as a harm. (5) Kaelyn's later emotionally abusive boyfriend and several guests' passing references to past trauma (Jez, Ilyse, Tiffany Reese, J.E.'s childhood slur) have no story, so they get no separate records and are noted in the relevant records. In quotations the catfisher's name is replaced with [perpetrator], and I chose quotations that name no non-victims. Two usage-limit interruptions caused no loss of reading: notes were written after each file.
